clue.text: Like the Duke of Edinburgh, soon had deer roundly shot

definitions.text: Like the Duke of Edinburgh, soon

indicators.note: shot in the sense of wrecked or worn out, so the three words that follow are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A royal tale: the Duke of Edinburgh lets fly at a stag on a shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: The Duke really did shoot game, which hides 'shot' as the anagram signal. When the puzzle appeared in December 2020 he was 99, so he would soon reach his centenary (he died in April 2021, two months short of it).
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Philip turned 99 in 2020, so a hundredth birthday was coming soon; the clue describes his age.

clue.text: Paint brush finally adapted into a device holding pillbox in place

indicators.note: finally picks out the last letter of the word brush
adapted means altered to fit, so the letters of paint plus one more are rearranged

explanation.surface: An artist's paintbrush is pressed into service to pin a pillbox hat on.
explanation.walkthrough: A pillbox is a small round hat, not a box for pills.
explanation.definitionFit: A long pin pushed through hat and hair keeps a pillbox hat steady on the head.

clue.text: Subtlety shown by woman of faith taking over a church

indicators.note: in a down entry, over puts the first part on top of the church
taking means the woman of faith holds the next piece inside her

parts.note: a nun is a woman in a religious order
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A religious woman takes charge of a church and shows subtlety.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine shade of meaning or a slight difference is a subtlety.

clue.text: Socialist hosts meeting that's organised and strictly regulated

indicators.note: hosts means the socialist holds the following letters within

parts.note: red is the usual label for a socialist or left-winger

indicators.note: organised here means put in order, telling us to rearrange the letters of meeting

explanation.surface: A left-winger chairs a well-run meeting that keeps to strict rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Regimented life is drilled, ordered and tightly controlled, like soldiers in a military unit.

clue.text: Live broadcast centre source

indicators.note: centre picks out the middle letter of the nine-letter word broadcast

parts.note: a well is a source of water, or figuratively of anything

explanation.surface: A live transmission from a broadcasting centre's main feed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live broadcast' wants to be read as a single phrase. In fact 'Live' is the definition, a verb meaning to reside.
explanation.definitionFit: To reside somewhere is to live there; the verb is used in phrases such as dwelling in a cottage.

clue.text: I note all clogs designed with cleats may be an exercise in futility

indicators.note: with joins the second part on after the first
designed means redesigned or remade, so the letters of the phrase before it are rearranged

parts.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written
cleats is literally a new castle: shuffle its letters and they spell castle, so the word stands for a new castle

explanation.surface: Clogs fitted with cleats, the speaker notes, may be a pointless project.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of I NOTE ALL CLOGS gives SELLING COAL TO. CLEATS is a 'new' (rearranged) CASTLE, which supplies the final word in a cryptic reading of its own. The usual idiom says carrying or taking coals; 'selling' is a variant.
explanation.definitionFit: Newcastle upon Tyne was a great coal port, so bringing it more fuel is a byword for pointless effort.

clue.text: Temporary abbreviation?

definitions.meaning: temporary means lasting only a little while
an abbreviation is a word cut down, in other words a term made short

explanation.definitionFit: Something temporary lasts briefly, and a shortened term is literally a short term.

clue.text: Left frequently in the attic

parts.note: oft is an old or poetic word for often

explanation.surface: Something stored away in the attic gets left there often.
explanation.definitionFit: The roof space of a house, used for storage, goes by either name.

clue.text: Chocolate after Colin passes out is elementary

indicators.note: passes out reads as Col passes out: both occurrences of the letters COL leave the joined string
after puts the sweet behind the name, so the name comes first

explanation.surface: Colin faints after eating chocolate, which is all very basic.
explanation.walkthrough: Write COLIN then CHOCOLATE, and remove both runs of COL ('passes out' read as the plural of 'col', a mountain pass). Colin fainting is the decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inchoate is only just begun and not yet developed, so it is rudimentary or elementary.

clue.text: Choice of words used by Lineker when admitting defeat

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so the footballer's first name takes the next word inside

parts.note: Gary Lineker is an English former footballer and TV presenter
a defeat is a loss

explanation.surface: The words a sports presenter picks when he has to concede that his side lost.
explanation.walkthrough: Gary Lineker is a former England striker who presents BBC football coverage.
explanation.definitionFit: A glossary is a list of selected terms with their meanings, a chosen set of vocabulary.

clue.text: Want reform before midnight, in a manner of speaking

indicators.note: before puts the reshaped word ahead of the last letter
reform means form again, so the letters of want are rearranged

parts.note: the middle of the word night is its letter G

explanation.surface: A campaigner wants reforms passed before midnight, in a manner of speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a manner of speaking' looks like a stock phrase. Here 'in' is a link and the rest is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A nasal or regional accent, such as a southern American drawl, is a distinctive way of talking.

clue.text: Due to position, previous lover gone and nice Dior clothing disappeared

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
off means gone, as in the milk is off or he is off

indicators.note: with the clothing gone, each of the two words loses its outer letters and keeps only its middle

explanation.surface: An ex-lover has left, and the nice Dior wardrobe has vanished too.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for by virtue of office: someone sits on a board automatically because of the post they hold.

clue.text: Partial earnings, please, must be included

indicators.note: must be included means the following letters go inside the earnings word

parts.note: earnings are income
split it as P and lease: P is the first letter, and lease becomes let, as in letting a house

explanation.surface: A worker asks to be paid at least part of their wages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Please' splits as P plus LEASE, and to lease a house is to LET it, giving PLET.
explanation.definitionFit: Something partial is not whole, lacking some part.

clue.text: Lackey of dodgy boss, mostly awful

indicators.note: awful means terrible, so the letters before it are made into a mess
mostly drops the final letter of the word boss

parts.note: taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: A boss's flunkey, for a shady and dreadful employer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dodgy' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder; 'awful' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A menial who does the drudge work for others is a lackey or general servant.

clue.text: With a plate he can certainly make the earth move

definitions.text: With a plate he can certainly make the earth move

parts.words: With a plate he can certainly make the earth move
parts.note: a tectonic plate off the Pacific Northwest named after a sixteenth-century navigator; plate movements cause earthquakes, and the Don Juan in the name hints at a lover

explanation.walkthrough: 'Make the earth move' is slang for a great sexual experience, and the name starts like Don Juan's. The literal reading is geology: a small Pacific plate whose movement causes earthquakes.
explanation.definitionFit: The plate is named after the navigator; plates slipping against each other is what shakes the ground.

clue.text: Either he's dead or my watch has stopped? Awkward question: run with it!

definitions.text: Either he's dead or my watch has stopped?

indicators.note: awkward means clumsy or ill-arranged, so the letters of the next words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Groucho Marx's quip on taking a pulse, then an awkward question with a jogging instruction.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening line is Groucho Marx's quip on taking a man's pulse, a conclusion that does not follow. 'With it' simply links the anagram to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The quoted joke is an example: a statement whose conclusion does not follow from what precedes it.

clue.text: See 5 across
She asks what might be necessary on a bicycle

indicators.note: asks means poses a question out loud, so we hear the spoken question

parts.words: what might be necessary on a bicycle
parts.note: a cyclist might ask whether a bell is required, phrased as a question beginning with is

explanation.surface: A woman asks what she might need for her bike.
explanation.walkthrough: The spoken question 'Is a bell?' sounds like the name. It echoes the old knock-knock joke ending 'Is a bell necessary on a bicycle?'
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name is one way to refer to a female, standing for she.

clue.text: Islands emphatically shut up about what some people do there

indicators.note: about means around, so the turned word goes around the next piece
in a down entry, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to slam a door is to shut it forcefully
visitors to the islands go scuba diving on the reefs

explanation.surface: Holidaymakers are firmly told to be quiet about their pastime in the islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shut up' reads as an order to be quiet, but 'up' is the reversal signal for the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An archipelago in the Indian Ocean, made up of coral atolls.

clue.text: An American politician?

parts.note: read differently, an American female citizen is a woman from the States, which also names a respected female political leader

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as 'States woman' and it describes any American woman. The question mark flags this pun on a word for a female political leader.
explanation.definitionFit: A respected and experienced female political leader, and literally a woman from the United States.

clue.text: See 5 across
Art student undressed on vacation, ready to breed

indicators.note: a word on vacation is emptied of its middle, so the art loses its central letter
undressed means stripped of clothing, so the student loses the letters at its tail end

explanation.surface: An art student strips off on holiday, eager to mate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' empties ART to AT. 'Undressed' strips the last three letters (ENT) from STUDENT, leaving STUD; that is a loose use, since undressed usually takes off both outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse kept for breeding is said to stand at stud, available to mate.

clue.text: See 12
One way to get salt when all else fails

parts.note: the answer, split and read as an instruction, means re-sort the word last, and its letters reordered spell salt

explanation.surface: A cook's tip for obtaining salt when nothing else works.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as an instruction: re-sort LAST, and its letters spell SALT.
explanation.definitionFit: A final fallback, the option kept until every other has failed.

clue.text: The asparagus served to you for starters is delicious

indicators.note: for starters means take the first letter of each word, with a culinary pun on the opening course

explanation.surface: A waiter serves asparagus as a starter, and it is delicious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For starters' fits the meal, but it tells you to take the first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that is delicious is good to eat, full of flavour.

clue.text: Part of sabbatical group

indicators.note: part of means only a section of the following word is used

explanation.surface: Taking a break from work is part of the band's routine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Swedish pop group, famous for 'Waterloo'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swedish pop band is a musical group, a band of performers.

clue.text: Evidence of passion from Elvis to be reviewed

indicators.note: reviewed read as re-viewed, looked at anew, so the letters are seen in a new order

explanation.surface: Signs of romance in Elvis's life are up for critical review.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reviewed' suggests a critic, but here it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Red marks left on the skin by passionate kissing or nipping are physical traces of ardour.

clue.text: 1 across the origin of light and dark

indicators.note: across means the first piece is laid over and around the next letter

parts.note: the number one is a unit

indicators.note: the origin of a word is where it begins, its first letter

explanation.surface: A cross-reference: the opening clue plus the source of light and darkness.
explanation.walkthrough: '1 across' looks like a reference to the clue at 1, but '1' here is a unit and 'across' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A room with no lamps switched on has no illumination, so it is dark.

clue.text: Trap set in earnest, leave it out

indicators.note: set means arranged, so the letters of the phrase are put into a fresh order once the it word is left out

explanation.surface: A trap has been set, earnestly; someone tells the setter to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave it out' is also British slang for 'stop that', which disguises the instruction to drop letters before 'set' rearranges the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensnare is to catch in a snare, so trap as a verb.

clue.text: See 1
